detail: Within 5% of the high counts as close to the top, and the S&P 500 closed at 7,619.38 on Wednesday, about 2.6% below its record close of 7,818.93 on 6 October. Wednesday's 1.3% rise narrowed the gap, a reminder that short wobbles of a few per cent are normal.
source: Cappnotes Closing Look and StockTitan closing figures, 11 Nov; record close from Anadolu and EdgeX, 6 Oct

detail: Breadth was broad on Wednesday: on the Nasdaq about 1.8 shares rose for every one that fell, and 17 S&P 500 members hit new 52-week highs with none at new lows. When most shares join in a rise, it rests on more than a handful of big names.
source: Cappnotes Closing Look (Nasdaq advancers and decliners, S&P 500 new highs and lows), 11 Nov

detail: Above 4.5% counts as high, and the US 10-year yield closed at about 4.98% on Tuesday, up roughly 10 basis points after the inflation figures, having briefly topped 5%. Safe government bonds paying close to 5% set a high bar for shares to beat.

Markets expect rates to go up: futures put about a 90% chance on a quarter-point Fed rise on 9 December, and roughly a two-in-three chance of another Bank of England rise on 17 December. Higher rates make borrowing dearer and tend to weigh on share prices, especially fast-growing companies.
source: CME FedWatch via CNBC and StockTitan, 11 Nov; Bank of England pricing via Pound Sterling Live, 11 Nov

detail: Above $90 a barrel counts as expensive, and Brent crude settled at $92.76 on Wednesday, up 1.4%, after Iran said its enriched nuclear material will not leave the country. Dear oil keeps pressure on inflation, which is one reason central banks are raising rates.
